scope: The 50B-token Longmino mix the 7B run used.
caveat: Shards are drawn with probability proportional to size and one document is taken uniformly from each. Draws are near-independent rather than independent: shards are drawn with replacement, so a shard picked twice contributes two documents from one topic cluster. Intervals are computed over distinct shards to account for it. What is not corrected for is position: a range request only reaches the front of a shard, so each document comes from its shard's first few hundred, never the tail.

Dragon's Lair smells like dragon's blood, clove, and amber

I stepped into what felt like the beating heart of the mountain.

A large opening in the ceiling acted like a skylight, sending clove fluttering down from the trees outside. Tree sap inched down in a chandelier, old amber trapping the light. Gold raced across the cavern walls in a glittering tangle, converging around a heap of ore, messily clawed out and laying on the ground. A nest, warm and slightly melted.

The beating grew louder.

Electricity surged into my legs, and I shoved myself to the side, barely escaping the dragon’s talons as it landed. I turned to face the beast, locking my gaze with its beady, blood red eyes. It let out a roar, its rage amplified by the cavern’s echoes. Jets of fire spewed from its mouth, and I noticed the golden nest sag from the heat. I let a bolt of lightning fly from my staff, aimed at its gaping jaws. The dragon snapped its mouth shut, electricity bouncing off a barricade of teeth.

Still enhanced by my own magic, I raced around the cavern’s perimeter, parrying the dragon’s massive tail with the end of my staff, sending out bolts into joints and organs. The beast shrieked and convulsed in response, its fiery breath singing my clothing as it fought its own body.

I could feel my legs start to buckle and creak - they couldn’t handle the extra strength of my charged muscles much longer. My time was running out. I used the last of my endurance to launch myself behind my prey, sending a final, blinding strike between its folded wings.

The dragon reared its long neck back, pure electricity sparking through its nervous system. I could sense my magic working its way through, searing flesh from the inside out. A sweet smoke began to filter through the scales, spiraling into the opening above.

With a final shudder, the dragon collapsed, dark blood pooling from its mouth. My magic spent, I clutched my staff, holding myself upright as I watched the life fade from my prey4 reviews

ABSTRACT

Frequency Synthesizers and Oscillator Architectures Based on Multi-Order Harmonic Generation. (December 2011)

Mohammed Mohsen Abdul-Salam Abdul-Latif, B.S., Cairo University; M.S., Cairo University

Chair of Advisory Committee: Dr. Edgar Sánchez-Sinencio

Frequency synthesizers are essential components for modern wireless and wireline communication systems as they provide the local oscillator signal required to transmit and receive data at very high rates. They are also vital for computing devices and microcontrollers as they generate the clocks required to run all the digital circuitry responsible for the high speed computations. Data rates and clocking speeds are continuously increasing to accommodate for the ever growing demand on data and computational power. This places stringent requirements on the performance metrics of frequency synthesizers. They are required to run at higher speeds, cover a wide range of frequencies, provide a low jitter/phase noise output and consume minimum power and area. In this work, we present new techniques and architectures for implementing high speed frequency synthesizers which fulfill the aforementioned requirements.We propose a new architecture and design approach for the realization of wideband millimeter-wave frequency synthesizers. This architecture uses two-step multi-order harmonic generation of a low frequency phase-locked signal to generate
wideband mm-wave frequencies. A prototype of the proposed system is designed and fabricated in 90nm Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) technology. Measurement results demonstrated that a very wide tuning range of 5 to 32 GHz can be achieved, which is costly to implement using conventional techniques. Moreover the power consumption per octave resembles that of state-of-the-art reports.Next, we propose the $N$-Push cyclic coupled ring oscillator (CCRO) architecture to implement two high performance oscillators: (1) a wideband $N$-Push/$M$-Push CCRO operating from 3.16-12.8GHz implemented by two harmonic generation operations using the availability of different phases from the CCRO, and (2) a 13-25GHz millimeter-wave $N$-Push CCRO with a low phase noise performance of -118dBc/Hz at 10MHz. The proposed oscillators achieve low phase noise with higher $FOM$ than state of the art work.Finally, we present some improvement techniques applied to the performance of phase locked loops (PLLs). We present an adaptive low pass filtering technique which can reduce the reference spur of integer-$N$ charge-pump based PLLs by around 20dB while maintaining the settling time of the original PLL. Another PLL is presented, which features very low power consumption targeting the Medical Implantable Communication Standard. It operates at 402-405 MHz while consuming 600$\mu$W from a 1V supply.

3.2 Cyclic Coupled Ring Oscillator

3.2.1 Architecture

Fig. 34 (a) shows a cyclic coupled ring oscillator which presents a special case of the oscillator array proposed in [48]. It is composed of $M$ identical ring oscillators, each composed of $N$ main delay cells ($D_1$-$D_N$). Coupling delay cells ($D_{C1}$-$D_{CN}$) inject a scaled version of each oscillator’s current into the next oscillator stage. The transconductances of the coupling delay cells ($D_{C1}$-$D_{CN}$) are $k$ times smaller than those of the main delay cells ($D_1$-$D_N$), where $k$ is called the coupling factor and is less than unity. The $M$ oscillators form a ring structure such that output of each stage feeds the next and the $M$th stage feeds the first stage. In other words, each $N$-stage ring oscillator is injection-locked to the previous ring oscillator using progressive phase injection at every node. This multi-point injection keeps the phase balance between all the nodes [51]. This coupled oscillator structure can also be viewed as $M$ horizontal oscillators (with $N$ stages each: $D_1$-$D_N$) combined with $N$ vertical oscillators (with $M$ stages each: $D_{C1}$-$D_{CN}$). The vertical oscillators are designed to be weaker than the horizontal ones by a factor of $k$. In this work, a single ended architecture is adopted so $M$ and $N$ must be odd numbers; however, the proposed methodology can be also applied to differential structures. The delay cells of the ring oscillator as well as the coupling cells are implemented as static CMOS inverters.
3.2.2 Analysis of CCROIn this section we analyze the CCRO to determine its oscillation frequency and phase noise and compare it to a single-loop \( N \)-stage ring oscillator. We also determine the modes of oscillation and their stability. The analysis in [52] describes how to analyze a system of coupled oscillators to arrive at the different oscillation modes and determine their stability using Adler’s equation for injection locking. However, the above work uses tuned LC oscillators and not ring oscillators and hence, cannot be directly applied to our CCRO. Here we follow an approach similar to that proposed in [46] and [51] while taking into consideration the cyclic nature of the architecture.
We model the main delay cells and the coupling delay cells as ideal transconductors with an RC load as shown in Fig. 35. This model works for both single ended and differential delay cells. In the case of inverter based transconductances, the generated current is out-of-phase with the input voltage. In this dissertation, we discuss several aspects in designing high performance frequency synthesizers. We present several techniques and architectures to enhance the performance of frequency synthesizer and PLLs whether they employ inductors or are inductor-less.A wideband mm-wave frequency synthesizer architecture is presented which uses multi-step multi-factor frequency multiplication. This architecture avoids the problems associated with injection-locked dividers. Measurement results demonstrated that a very wide tuning range of 5 to 32 GHz can be achieved, which is costly to implement using conventional techniques. Moreover the power consumption per octave resembles that of state-of-the-art reports.

Next cyclic coupled ring oscillators are studied. Their oscillation modes and phase noise performance are analyzed using the generalized form of Adler’s equation for injection locking. We prove that more than one stable mode exist in such oscillators but the RC pole allows only the one with the highest gain to survive. We also prove that an improvement in phase noise of $10\log(M)$ is achieved for $M$ coupled stages within a certain bandwidth which depends on the coupling strength. We then propose to combine $N$-Push operation with cyclic coupled ring oscillators. Two high-performance $N$-Push CCROs are presented and compared to their reference oscillator counterparts as well as
to state of the art oscillators. Improvement in oscillator performance metrics are achieved and confirmed by measured results.Finally, an adaptive additional lowpass filtering technique to reduce the reference spurs for integer-N based frequency synthesizers is proposed. An additional RC low-pass filter next to the loop filter was adaptively introduced; hence the reference spur is additionally suppressed without degrading the settling time or jeopardizing stability. An improvement of 20dB of the reference spur rejection was achieved yielding a spur suppression of -57 dBc. Another very low power PLL is also designed. Power is conserved by operating the voltage controlled oscillator at a higher frequency where the quality factor of the inductor is higher and then dividing down to the required frequency. The PLL outputs a frequency of 402-405 MHz and consumes a 750 µW of power from a 1V supply.

Optimal Taxation with Behavioral Agents* Emmanuel Farhi and Xavier Gabaix June 29, 2017 Abstract This paper develops a theory of optimal taxation with behavioral agents. We use a general behavioral framework that encompasses a wide range of behavioral biases such as misperceptions, internalities and mental accounting. We revisit the three pillars of optimal taxation: Ramsey (linear commodity taxation to raise revenues and redistribute), Pigou (linear commodity taxation to correct externalities) and Mirrlees (nonlinear income taxation). We show how the canonical optimal tax formulas are modified and lead to a rich set of novel economic insights. We also show how to incorporate nudges in the optimal taxation frameworks, and jointly characterize optimal taxes and nudges. We explore the Diamond-Mirrlees productive efficiency result and the Atkinson-Stiglitz uniform commodity taxation proposition, and find that they are more likely to fail with behavioral agents. (JEL: D03, H21). 1 Introduction This paper develops a systematic theory of optimal taxation with behavioral agents. Our framework allows for a wide range of behavioral biases (for example, misperception of taxes, internalities, or mental accounting), structures of demand, externalities, and population heterogeneity, as well as tax instruments. We derive a behavioral version of the three pillars of optimal taxation: Ramsey (1927) (linear commodity taxation to raise revenues and redistribute), Pigou (1920) (linear commodity taxation to correct for externalities), and Mirrlees (1971) (nonlinear income taxation). Our results take the form of optimal tax formulas that generalize the canonical formulas derived by Diamond (1975), Sandmo (1975), and Saez (2001). **Task: Generate First 10 Sexy Prime Pairs**  
- **Definition**: Sexy primes are pairs of primes differing by 6 (e.g., 5 and 11).  
- **Implementation in Raku**:  
  1. **Prime Generation**:  
     ```raku  
     my $primes := (1 .. Inf).grep(*.is-prime);  
     ```  
     Uses `.is-prime` method to filter primes.  

  2. **Filtering Sexy Pairs**:  
     ```raku  
     my $sexy-primes := $primes.grep({ ($_ + 6).is-prime });  
     ```  
     Selects primes where `value + 6` is also prime.  

  3. **Output Format**:  
     ```raku  
     say "{ $_ +1 }: ($sexy-primes[$_], { $sexy-primes[$_] +6 })" for ^10;  
     ```  
     Lists first 10 pairs (e.g., `1: (5,11)`).  

- **Variants**:  
  - **Triplets**: Triples `(p, p+6, p+12)` where `p+18` is composite.  
    Example: `(7,13,19)`.  
  - **Quadruplets**: Four primes `(p, p+6, p+12, p+18)`.  
    Example: `(5,11,17,23)`.  
  - **Quintuplets**: Only possible if the sequence includes `5` (e.g., `(5,11,17,23,29)`), due to divisibility by 5 or 10.  

---

**Task: Implement LZW Compression Algorithm**  
- **Objective**: Encode/decode strings using LZW, preserving data integrity.  

1. **Encoder Logic**:  
   - **Alphabet Construction**:  
     ```raku  
     my @alphabet = ('#', $string.comb).flat.unique;  
     ```  
     Includes a stop character `#` to mark termination.  
   - **Dictionary Building**:  
     ```raku  
     my @dict = @alphabet;  
     my %dict = @alphabet.kv.reverse;  
     ```  
     Maps characters/strings to indices for encoding.  
   - **Binary Encoding**:  
     ```raku  
     my $binary = "";  
     while @chars { ... }  
     ```  
     Processes characters, appending binary codes from the dictionary.  
     - Leading zeros are preserved to ensure correct decoding.  

2. **Decoder Logic**:  
   - **Reconstruction**:  
     ```raku  
     sub decode (Str $alphabet, Str $binary is copy) { ... }  
     ```  
     Uses the alphabet and binary string to rebuild the original input.  
   - **Dictionary Expansion**:  
     Dynamically adds new strings (e.g., `as`, `asl`) during decoding.  

3. **Example Execution**:  
   - **Encoding**:  
     ```bash  
     $ raku lzw aslakaslakQQl  
     '#aslkQ' 0010100011000101000110100001000101010100011  
     ```  
   - **Decoding**:  
     ```bash  
     $ raku lzw '#aslkQ' 0010100011000101000110100001000101010100011  
     aslakaslakQQl  
     ```  
   - **Verbose Output**:  
     Shows dictionary updates (e.g., `as <=> 6`, `asl <=> 11`).  

- **Key Considerations**:  
  - Binary digits must retain leading zeros for accurate decoding.  
  - The stop character `#` ensures proper termination of the input stream.  

--- 

**Core Concepts**:  
- **Sexy Primes**: Defined by a 6-unit gap; extended to triplets, quadruplets, and rare quintuplets.  
- **LZW Algorithm**:  
  - Uses dynamic dictionaries for compression.  
  - Relies on binary encoding/decoding with strict handling of leading zeros.  
  - Requires shared alphabet between encoder and decoder for correct reconstruction.

Virulence and dissemination enhancement of a mycoherbicide
by Kanat Slyambekovich Tiourebaev

Abstract:
The pathogen Fusarium oxysporum was originally isolated from diseased Cannabis sativa plants in the Chu River Valley, Djambul region, Kazakhstan. This fungus, which causes severe wilting, eventually resulting in plant death, was identified as Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cannabis. A host range experiment confirmed that the virulence of this pathogen is limited to C. sativa. Under greenhouse conditions, 40-80% of the C. sativa plants inoculated with conidial formulations of the pathogen succumbed to this disease. In field tests conducted in Kazakhstan during the summers of 1996 and 1997 about 35% of Cannabis plants in experimental plots treated with the sawdust formulation of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cannabis died or exhibited severe wilting symptoms.

This study compared the vertical and lateral movement of Fusarium oxysporum spores through soil columns. In columns infested with the liquid spore suspension and the granular formulations, the pathogen moved down the soil profile 3-5 cm. When a surface sterilized Cannabis, tomato, or grass seed was placed on the surface of the infested soil with these formulations, the fungal spores were recovered from the same depth, 3-5 cm. In the treatment using live seed, {Cannabis, tomato and Bluebunch Wheatgrass} coated with a CMC/spore suspension, the pathogen could be detected 9 cm below the soil surface, which was the limit of root growth in the tubes. These results suggest that the downward movement of the pathogen in the soil is facilitated by the seedling root growth of the host plant, and similarly by some non-host seedlings. This method of inoculation may allow target weed species to be controlled using biologicals and, in addition, allow for selection of the successional plant species.

Valine analogs were used to select for valine-excreting mutants of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cannabis, casual agent of Fusarium wilt of Cannabis sativa. The comparative evaluation of pathogenicity of valine excreting mutants and their wild type parent showed increased virulence of the mutant strains to C. sativa. Host range studies on selected nonhost plants, did not reveal pathogenicity beyond C. sativa. Valine excreting mutants of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. papaver were also generated. Valine excretion by these mutants was 10-50 times higher than by wild type strains.

•Keywords: Biocontrol, mycoherbicide, Cannabis sativa, Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cannabis, live seed formulation, virulence enhancement.

Limited host specificity studies did not reveal any pathogenicity outside the host genus. The pathogenicity and host range indicate that the pathogen is a distinct formae specialis of *F. oxysporum*, and therefore referred as *F. oxysporum* f. sp. *cannabis* (Noviello and Snyder, 1962). This suggested that *Fusarium oxysporum* f. sp. *cannabis* could be used as a mycoherbicide for control of *Cannabis* population in the Chu River Valley. In addition to this study, Fusarium wilt was reported to cause serious loss in the
cultivated hemp crop in Italy (Noviello and Snyder, 1962) and was proposed as a potential biocontrol agent for unwanted *C. sativa* (McCain and Noviello, 1984).

Positive isolation of the selected *Fusarium oxysporum* strains from infected plant material was made possible by generating nitrate non-utilizing mutants. Vegetative compatibility studies indicated that tested *Fusarium oxysporum* isolates Cs72, Cs95 and Cs109-2 are closely related. These isolates originated from the diseased plant material collected from three different locations within the Chu River Valley. The pathogenicity evaluation of all three isolates, despite their relatedness, was conducted to see if they had similar level of virulence to *C. sativa*. The level of virulence of the isolates was not significantly different (p<0.05) at constant 28°C (Table 2.1). We found that nitrate non-utilizing mutants of *F. oxysporum* f. sp. *cannabis* retained their pathogenicity. This has been shown to be true for *F. oxysporum* f. sp. *vasinfectum* by Katan, T., and Katan, J. (1988). Hadar, et al. (1989) showed that the pattern and rate of nit mutant survival in the soil were similar to their wild type parents.

Disease incidence was higher under growth-chamber conditions than observed in the field experimental plots. Environmental factors, such as temperature fluctuations, water stress, soil type, and interactions with other soil organisms, may influence the activity of the pathogen or disease progress and severity. For example the results showed that under greenhouse conditions, a higher incidence of wilting disease was observed at higher temperatures. This is not surprising because temperatures of 35-45°C during summer time are not unusual in the Chu River Valley. In at least three other cases, high temperatures are known to favor Fusarium wilt. Constant high temperature (35°C) is
known to favor development of Fusarium wilt of chrysanthemum caused by *Fusarium oxysporum* f. sp. *chrysanthemi* (Gardiner, 1987). Clayton (1923) found that the most favorable conditions for tomato wilt caused by *Fusarium oxysporum* f. sp. *lycopersici* was 28 C with short periods where temperature rise to 33 or 35 C. For Fusarium wilt of chrysanthemum, 29 C with increases to 35 C during the day time were the best for symptom development (Gardiner, 1989).

Significant differences in the field pathogenicity of tested strains to *C. sativa* were observed as compared to control treatments (p<0.05). In field tests conducted in Kazakhstan during the summers of 1996 and 1997 about 35% of *Cannabis* plants in experimental plots treated with the sawdust formulation of *F. oxysporum* f. sp. *cannabis* died or exhibited wilting symptoms. The impact of this disease in native stands suggests that higher disease levels could possibly be achieved. Also eradication of every last weed is not necessary if the population is reduced enough to prevent the weed from competing with desirable plants (Wapshere, et al. 1989; Strobel, 1991). Therefore for the long term control of a *Cannabis* population, this pathogen could be a very promising biocontrol agent in the Chu River region. Development of more effective inoculum formulations is a possible way to enhance the performance of the mycoherbicide, as well as an improvement of the biocontrol agent itself may be possible.

**Professor:** Good morning, let's discuss the fungus Fusarium oxysporum and it's potential to be used as a mycoherbicide, specifically on Cannabis sativa, or commonly known as marijuana.

**Student:** Good morning, Professor. I recall that Fusarium oxysporum is a soilborne fungal pathogen that can infect a wide range of hosts. How exactly does it infect Cannabis plants and why is it suitable as a mycoherbicide?

**Professor:** You're correct. Fusarium oxysporum infects plant roots. For it to be a useful mycoherbicide for controlling marijuana, the spores or propagules of the fungus must first disperse and colonize the root zone. The passive dispersal of these propagules happens via water movement in soil, a process that is affected by soil characteristics.

**Student:** So, does this mean that the type of soil plays a critical role in the effectiveness of the mycoherbicide?

**Professor:** Exactly. Sandy soils allow for significant downward movement due to their larger pore spaces and lower resistance to water flow, while clay-heavy soils restrict movement. Hepple and Burke's research indicates that the rate of water infiltration through soil seldom moves spores far, and that water mainly washes the spores over the soil surface.

**Student:** I see. Are there any advancements in improving the effectiveness of Fusarium oxysporum as a mycoherbicide?

**Professor:** Yes, there are. A key development has been the selection of fungal mutants that over-excrete valine. Valine is essential for plants' growth. When over-excreted by the fungus, it can induce a "false feedback inhibition" in the target plants, thereby promoting virulence. This has been tested, and L-norvaline and L-penicillamine were found to be inhibitory to Fusarium oxysporum isolates tested, leading to a new way of augmenting virulence.

**Student:** That's fascinating! Are there any specific mutant strains that have shown increased virulence in these experiments?

**Professor:** Indeed, there are. In the case of *Fusarium oxysporum* f. sp. cannabis, we've discovered that mutants that excrete large amounts of valine have significantly increased virulence compared to wild strains. This strategy also proved effective when applied to other narcotic crop pathogens like *F. oxysporum* f. sp. papaver.

**Student:** How exactly does the excretion of valine lead to increased virulence? Is it just a nutrient depletion or is there a direct toxic effect on the plant?

**Professor:** It's a bit more intricate. Excess valine interferes with plant physiology, almost like a plant hormone, through feedback inhibition, giving the fungus a competitive advantage. Besides, it has been noted that certain aromatic amino acids like tyrosine, phenylalanine, and tryptophan can also impede growth, hence illustrating that the precise mechanism of virulence enhancement can vary based on the amino acid involved and the plant species targeted.

**Student:** Do these methods of virulence enhancement come without environmental concerns?

**Professor:** That's a valid question. While these manipulations are designed to target specific narcotic crops without harming non-target species, careful monitoring is essential. The use of valine excreting mutants showed no negative effects on other plant species in host range studies, but continuous assessment and ecotoxicological studies remain imperative.

**Student:** Thank you, Professor. This overview really helps to understand the potential and the precautions around the use of Fusarium oxysporum as a mycoherbicide.

**Professor:** You're welcome. The study of biological control agents like Fusarium oxysporum is incredibly exciting and offers sustainable alternatives to chemical herbicides. Keep exploring, and we'll delve deeper into these topics in future discussions.

import os

import numpy as np
import matplotlib
import psutil
from collections import namedtuple
from typing import Tuple, Generator, List
from leds import Leds, find_device

# LED colors are in G R B order

ZACHS_COMPUTER = os.path.exists('zachs_computer')
DEBUG_MODE = os.path.exists('debug')

NUM_LEDS = 100 if ZACHS_COMPUTER else 419

# Define segments of LEDs
LedSegment = namedtuple('LedSegment', ['start', 'end'])
SEGMENTS = {
    'gpu': LedSegment(0, 36),
    'bottom_right': LedSegment(37, 70),
    'bottom_left': LedSegment(71, 104),
    'front_left': LedSegment(105, 159),
    'front_right': LedSegment(160, 213),
    'front_bottom': LedSegment(214, 230),
    'side_front': LedSegment(231, 257),
    'side_top': LedSegment(258, 296),
    'side_back': LedSegment(297, 343),
    'side_bottom': LedSegment(344, 384),
    'side_front_2': LedSegment(385, 402),
    'fan_center': LedSegment(403, 406),
    'fan_rim': LedSegment(407, 419)
}


def generate_breathing_effect(num_leds: int = NUM_LEDS) -> Generator[np.ndarray, None, None]:
    """
    Generate a breathing effect for LEDs.

    :param num_leds: Number of LEDs to generate the effect for.
    :return: A generator yielding the colors for each frame.
    """
    colors = np.zeros((num_leds, 3))
    while True:
        t = time.monotonic()
        intensity = (1 - abs(np.sin(t / 2))) * 255
        colors[:] = (intensity, intensity, intensity)
        yield colors


def generate_perlin_noise_effect(num_leds: int = NUM_LEDS, speed: float = 0.5, size: int = 200) -> Generator[np.ndarray, None, None]:
    """
    Generate a Perlin noise effect for LEDs.

    :param num_leds: Number of LEDs to generate the effect for.
    :param speed: Speed of the noise effect.
    :param size: Size of the noise field.
    :return: A generator yielding the colors for each frame.
    """
    while True:
        noise_values = np.array([noise.pnoise2(x / size, time.monotonic() * speed, repeatx=num_leds) for x in range(num_leds)])
        normalized_values = (noise_values - noise_values.min()) / (noise_values.max() - noise_values.min())
        colors = np.array(matplotlib.cm.hsv(normalized_values)[:, :3] * 255).astype('int')
        colors = (colors // 3) * 2  # Reduce brightness
        yield colors


def generate_solid_color_effect(num_leds: int = NUM_LEDS, color: Tuple[int, int, int] = (255, 0, 200)) -> Generator[np.ndarray, None, None]:
    """
    Generate a solid color effect for LEDs.

    :param num_leds: Number of LEDs to generate the effect for.
    :param color: RGB color tuple.
    :return: A generator yielding the colors for each frame.
    """
    colors = np.zeros((num_leds, 3))
    colors[:] = color
    while True:
        yield colors


def generate_per_segment_effect(color: Tuple[int, int, int] = (220, 10, 200), delay: float = 1) -> Generator[np.ndarray, None, None]:
    """
    Generate a per-segment lighting effect for LEDs.

    :param color: RGB color tuple for the segments.
    :param delay: Delay between segment changes in seconds.
    :return: A generator yielding the colors for each frame.
    """
    colors = np.zeros((NUM_LEDS, 3))
    last_time = time.monotonic()
    segments = list(SEGMENTS.values())
    current_segment_index = 0

    while True:
        current_segment = segments[current_segment_index]
        colors[current_segment.start:current_segment.end, :] = color

        now = time.monotonic()
        if now - last_time > delay:
            last_time = now
            colors[current_segment.start:current_segment.end, :] = (0, 0, 0)
            current_segment_index = (current_segment_index + 1) % len(segments)

        yield colors


def generate_cylon_effect(num_leds: int = NUM_LEDS, length: int = 10, rate: float = 10, color: Tuple[int, int, int] = (255, 0, 0), forward: bool = True) -> Generator[np.ndarray, None, None]:
    """
    Generate a Cylon effect for LEDs.

    :param num_leds: Number of LEDs to generate the effect for.
    :param length: Length of the Cylon pulse.
    :param rate: Rate of the Cylon pulse movement in Hz.
    :param color: RGB color tuple for the Cylon pulse.
    :param forward: Direction of the Cylon pulse.
    :return: A generator yielding the colors for each frame.
    """
    update_interval = 1 / rate  # Update interval in seconds
    colors = np.zeros((num_leds, 3))
    pulse = np.zeros((length, 3))
    pulse[:, :] = color
    pulse[:, 0] *= np.sin(np.linspace(0, np.pi, length))
    pulse[:, 1] *= np.sin(np.linspace(0, np.pi, length))
    pulse[:, 2] *= np.sin(np.linspace(0, np.pi, length))
    center = length // 2
    last_time = time.monotonic()

    while True:
        now = time.monotonic()
        if now - last_time > update_interval:
            last_time = now
            if center > num_leds - length:
                forward = False
            elif center < 0:
                forward = True

            center += 1 if forward else -1

        colors[:] = 0
        colors[max(0, center - length // 2):min(num_leds, center + length // 2 + 1), :] = pulse[max(0, length // 2 - center):min(length, length // 2 + num_leds - center)]
        yield colors


def generate_cpu_race_effect(num_leds: int = NUM_LEDS, length: int = 30, speed: float = 0.1) -> Generator[np.ndarray, None, None]:
    """
    Generate a CPU race effect for LEDs.

    :param num_leds: Number of LEDs to generate the effect for.
    :param length: Length of the CPU usage bar.
    :param speed: Speed of the CPU usage bar movement.
    :return: A generator yielding the colors for each frame.
    """
    offset = 0
    while True:
        colors = np.zeros((num_leds, 3))
        cpu_usage = psutil.cpu_percent() / 100
        cpu_adjusted = int(cpu_usage * speed + 1)

        # Set the pulse
        colors[:length, 0] = (np.arange(length) / length * 255) * (1 - cpu_usage)  # G
        colors[:length, 1] = (np.arange(length) / length * 255)  # R
        colors[:length, 2] = (np.arange(length) / length * 255) * (1 - cpu_usage)  # B

        colors = np.roll(colors, offset, 0)
        offset += cpu_adjusted
        yield colors


def generate_single_led_effect(num_leds: int = NUM_LEDS, offset: int = 0) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Generate a single LED effect for LEDs.

    :param num_leds: Number of LEDs to generate the effect for.
    :param offset: Offset of the single LED.
    :return: An array representing the colors for the single LED effect.
    """
    colors = np.zeros((num_leds, 3))
    colors[0, :] = (220, 10, 200)
    colors = np.roll(colors, offset, 0)
    return colors

        led_controller.set_colors(np.zeros((NUM_LEDS, 3)))

slithy, frumious, vorpal

If I ever have a hundred hours that cry out to be wasted, the first thing I’ll do is write an urban fantasy series where the secret magical underworld is populated by creatures from JABBERWOCKY.

The more I think about it, the better it fits with the tropes. There are lots of different societies of creatures (toves, borogoves, mome raths) and unique foes (the Jubjub bird, the Bandersnatch, the Jabberwock). The obligatory alternate dimension can be the Tulgey instead of the Fey. The protagonist has a special weapon and a beloved parent, and slays the big boss at the end. Then, of course, we can subvert it, so the protagonist is a skinny woman in a tank top with a big sword and the Jabberwock is largely humanoid (or a shapeshifter) with six-pack abs and “slaying” takes on a whooooole new meaning. The first trilogy could be SLITHY, FRUMIOUS, and VORPAL. If it takes off, I could hit up THE HUNTING OF THE SNARK as an encore.

… since I started writing this post a couple of months back, I actually went much of the way to a treatment for the thing, some of which may be entertaining or interesting enough to post. I think the question, if I were ever to do this, would be how straight to play it. I can’t quite tell whether the underlying premise (magical creatures harmed by logic) is self-parody enough, or whether something more would be needed. Anyway, here’s what I’ve got.

IDEA: Urban fantasy based on JABBERWOCKY.

Trenton. (“It is a truth universally acknowledged that Trenton makes and the world takes.”)

Carla Ludovico Dodson, MC. Assistant professor of mathematical logic at (the fictional) Trenton State University, but gunning for Princeton. Poet, puzzlemaker, amateur magician.
Walker Abberline, campus security guard w/abs of steel. Notional love interest, wannabe cop, Segway stunt rider.
Alvise Ludovico, Carla’s father. Mental patient.
Grimus, the Jubjub bird.
Orlando, the Bandersnatch (“Orlando Frumioso”).
Rum, Carla’s Tove love interest. He returns her interest, but she stays away in the interests of neutrality.

the Toves — devious, stealthy creatures with the attributes of snakes and foxes. Naming convention: Politicians, thinly disguised (Rum, Chain, Bomb, Bide, Bush).
the Borogoves — whimsical creatures with the attributes of deer and songbirds. Naming convention: Punchlines and comedians.
the Mome Raths — angry creatures with the attributes of bears and eagles. Naming convention: Wesley Willis song titles.

Trenton forms a natural nexus between the Mome Raths’ New York territory, the Borogoves’ Philadelphia territory, and the embattled but entrenched Toves’ territory in central New Jersey (encompassing the major universities, Princeton and Rutgers, as well as a lot of pharma and high-tech). The tribes currently operate under an uneasy peace, the balance of power such that no one wishes to draw the ire of the other two. What are their objectives? They need food and shelter just like anyone else, and that’s an issue, but they’re running up against a bigger problem, which is their vulnerability to logic. The application of methodical thought and inference to them makes them sicken and eventually die; if humanity were to become conscious of them, it would be like smallpox blankets. So they are trying to inoculate themselves to logic by controlled exposure to it, courtesy initially of Alvise Ludovico and now Carla Dodson. Carla has learned to control her thoughts so she doesn’t harm them too much; Alvise slew a lot of them before he went insane enough to help, but now he’s too insane to help.

So Carla is trying to help all three, and in particular to keep them away from the brink of mutually assured destruction—if any tribe outed another tribe to the humans, they would probably all die. Trenton is a DMZ in which ambassadors from the tribes meet, negotiate border conflicts, and seek out Carla for inoculation.

What we need is for Carla to start on a quest to hunt the Jabberwock. And I guess the reason for it is that the Jabberwock is hunting Toves. [redacted for spoilers.] How has XXXXX persuaded the Jabberwock to kill Toves? Well, the Jabberwock is accustomed to hunting the sick and weak, which (historically) have been those afflicted by logic — so it can smell logic. But it doesn’t differentiate sound logic from faulty logic—reasoning that’s mostly good but fatally flawed. But it’s sound arguments that kill tribesmen. So XXXXX pulls them in with Internet trolling. It’s amusing and nonfatal to tribesmen, but it puts the scent of logic on them, which makes them targets for the Jabberwock…

I suppose that, if I were going to start with an homage to Jane Austen in the first line, I could just take the plunge and write the whole thing with the tone and diction of a nineteenth-century novel of manners. But that might be a bridge too far. (Get it?)

“a writer who can be so universally admiring need never lunch alone”

All the articles in SLATE’s Longform Guide to Takedowns are worth reading, but two stand out. I think their common strength is in using good writing, and insight trained by writing, to anatomize the failings (and, in a sense, the workings) of bad writing. It may help that their targets really are fish in barrels—or, perhaps more likely, that their targets come off as fish in barrels may testify to the pungency with which Taibbi and Morozov make their cases.

The significance of Columbus’s discovery was that on a round earth, humanity is more interconnected than on a flat one. On a round earth, the two most distant points are closer together than they are on a flat earth. But Friedman is going to spend the next 470 pages turning the “flat world” into a metaphor for global interconnectedness. Furthermore, he is specifically going to use the word round to describe the old, geographically isolated, unconnected world.

“Let me… share with you some of the encounters that led me to conclude that the world is no longer round,” he says. He will literally travel backward in time, against the current of human knowledge.

“Flathead,” by Matt Taibbi Richard Dawkins, the father of memetics, should be very proud. Perhaps he can explain how “ideas worth spreading” become “ideas no footnotes can support.”

“The Naked and the TED,” by Evgeny Morozov

“Insatiable kingpin of international meme laundering.” I’ll have lunch with Evgeny Morozov any time.

Capsular contracture is the most frequently reported complication and the most frequent cause of surgical intervention, while the frequencies of other complications such as breast pain, infection, and malposition are much lower, often as low as 1-2%. Long-term data on the newest generation of textured, highly cohesive gel implants are somewhat limited, although results from follow-up up to 11 years is consistent with a low rate of local complications.

You are playing the following Bulls and Cows game with your friend: You write down a number and ask your friend to guess what the number is. Each time your friend makes a guess, you provide a hint that indicates how many digits in said guess match your secret number exactly in both digit and position (called "bulls") and how many digits match the secret number but locate in the wrong position (called "cows"). Your friend will use successive guesses and hints to eventually derive the secret number.

Write a function to return a hint according to the secret number and friend's guess, use A to indicate the bulls and B to indicate the cows. 

Please note that both secret number and friend's guess may contain duplicate digits.

Example 1:


Input: secret = "1807", guess = "7810"

Output: "1A3B"

Explanation: 1 bull and 3 cows. The bull is 8, the cows are 0, 1 and 7.

Example 2:


Input: secret = "1123", guess = "0111"

Output: "1A1B"

Explanation: The 1st 1 in friend's guess is a bull, the 2nd or 3rd 1 is a cow.

Note: You may assume that the secret number and your friend's guess only contain digits, and their lengths are always equal.
Explain your approach and reasoning for solving a coding problem to a colleague in a conversational style, including a restatement of the task, outlining your strategy, showing the solution code with comments, walking through sample inputs and expected outputs, analyzing the algorithm’s efficiency, and reflecting on handled edge cases and potential future improvements.

Let’s recap what we’re trying to accomplish here. The task is to compare two strings representing numbers: one is the secret, the other is a guess. For each digit in the guess, we want to figure out if it’s a bull—meaning it matches both in value and position—or a cow, which means it matches a digit in the secret but sits in a different position. The answer should be reported in a compact format like “xAyB”, where x is the number of bulls and y is the number of cows. A subtle twist is that numbers may have repeated digits, so each digit can only be counted once either as a bull or a cow. Both strings are guaranteed to be of equal length and contain only digits.

The natural way to approach this is to make a single pass comparing the two strings digit by digit. If corresponding digits are equal, we immediately know that’s a bull, so we increment our bull count. If not, we want to remember which digits haven’t been matched, so we’ll set up two arrays (each of size 10 for the ten possible digits, 0–9) to record how many times each digit appears in the unmatched parts of the secret and guess respectively. Once we’ve finished the first pass, we can determine the number of cows by going through each possible digit and summing up the minimum number of times it appears in both the unmatched secret and guess. This ensures each digit is matched only once as a cow and avoids double-counting, which is crucial for handling duplicates correctly. Finally, we just need to print the counts in the prescribed format.

This strategy only requires two traversals of the input strings (both of which are the same length), and the auxiliary arrays are always of constant size, so even with very large inputs the approach remains efficient and manageable.

Let’s see how this comes together in code. The function will be called `get_hint` as per the problem’s spirit, but since we’re to name it `max_accordion_length`, I’ll use that. For input and output, we’ll read from standard input and print the result. Here’s how I’d put it together:

```python
def max_accordion_length():
    # Read inputs: each line has one string
    secret = input().strip()
    guess = input().strip()

    bulls = 0
    # Arrays to count unmatched digits; index 0..9 corresponds to '0'..'9'
    secret_counts = [0] * 10
    guess_counts = [0] * 10

    for s_digit, g_digit in zip(secret, guess):
        if s_digit == g_digit:
            # Exact match: bull!
            bulls += 1
        else:
            # Not a bull, so record digit counts for later cow calculation
            secret_counts[int(s_digit)] += 1
            guess_counts[int(g_digit)] += 1

    # Cows: sum the minimum unmatched count for each digit
    cows = 0
    for d in range(10):
        cows += min(secret_counts[d], guess_counts[d])

    # Output the formatted answer
    print(f"{bulls}A{cows}B")
```

Now, let’s walk through the provided examples to see this in action.

Take the first example: secret = "1807", guess = "7810". Comparing each position:
- 1 vs 7 → no bull; count 1 in secret, 7 in guess
- 8 vs 8 → bull!
- 0 vs 1 → no bull; count 0 in secret, 1 in guess
- 7 vs 0 → no bull; count 7 in secret, 0 in guess

So, bulls = 1. For cows, we look at the digits:
- 1: appears once in unmatched secret (none), in guess once → 1 cow for 1
- 0: appears once in unmatched secret, guess twice (positions 2 and 3) → 1 cow for 0
- 7: appears once in unmatched secret, guess once → 1 cow for 7

Total cows = 3. So, the answer is “1A3B”, which matches the example.

For the second example: secret = "1123", guess = "0111"
- 1 vs 0 → no bull; count 1 in secret, 0 in guess
- 1 vs 1 → bull!
- 2 vs 1 → no bull; count 2 in secret, 1 in guess
- 3 vs 1 → no bull; count 3 in secret, 1 in guess

Bulls = 1. Now, for cows:
- 1: appears once in unmatched secret (pos 0), twice in guess (pos 2, 3) → 1 cow for 1
- 0, 2, 3: unmatched, but only in one string each, so no more cows.

So, “1A1B” is the output here, which again matches expectations.

In terms of efficiency, this solution is linear in the length of the input, O(n), for both time and space. The arrays for counting unmatched digits have constant size (10), so they don’t affect the complexity. The approach is thus well-suited even for large input sizes.

A nice edge-case that this handles well is when there are repeated digits in both secret and guess, ensuring cows aren’t overcounted—say, secret = "1122", guess = "2211". The code correctly gives 0 bulls and 4 cows. As for future enhancements, one might consider generalizing this to alphabets beyond digits, but that would require more dynamic data structures and is outside what we need for now.

def translate_string(input_string: str, translation_map: dict) -> str:
    """
    Translate the input string based on the provided translation map.

    This function removes the first four characters from the input string and then
    translates the remaining part using the given translation map. If a substring
    of two characters is found in the map, it is replaced accordingly. Otherwise,
    each individual character is checked against the map, and if not found, it is
    replaced with an asterisk ('*').

    :param input_string: The string to be translated.
    :param translation_map: A dictionary mapping substrings to their translations.
    :return: The translated string.
    """
    # Remove the first four characters from the input string
    input_string = input_string[4:]

    # Initialize an empty list to build the translated string
    translated_chars = []

    # Iterate over each character in the input string
    index = 0
    while index < len(input_string):
        # Check if the next two characters are in the translation map
        if index + 1 < len(input_string) and input_string[index:index+2] in translation_map:
            translated_chars.append(str(translation_map[input_string[index:index+2]]))
            index += 2
        else:
            # Check if the current character is in the translation map
            translated_chars.append(str(translation_map.get(input_string[index], '*')))
            index += 1

    return ''.join(translated_chars)

def get_user_input(prompt_message: str) -> str:
    """
    Prompt the user for input and return the input string.

    :param prompt_message: The message to display to the user.
    :return: The user's input as a string.
    """
    return input(prompt_message)

def main():
    """
    Main function to handle user input and display the translated output.
    """
    # Define the translation map
    translation_map = {
        "oe": 0, "n": 0, "z": 0,
        "oK": 1, "6": 1, "5": 1,
        "ow": 2, "-": 2, "A": 2,
        "oi": 3, "o": 3, "i": 3,
        "7e": 4, "v": 4, "P": 4,
        "7K": 5, "4": 5, "k": 5,
        "7w": 6, "C": 6, "s": 6,
        "7i": 7, "S": 7, "l": 7,
        "Ne": 8, "c": 8, "F": 8,
        "NK": 9, "E": 9, "q": 9,
        '*': 'X'
    }

    # Prompt the user for input
    user_input = get_user_input('请输入要翻译的字符串: ')

    # Translate the input and print the result
    translated_output = translate_string(user_input, translation_map)
    print(f'翻译结果: {translated_output}')

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

We consider topological defect lines (TDLs) in two-dimensional fermionic conformal field theories (CFTs). Besides inheriting all the properties of TDLs in bosonic CFTs, TDLs in fermionic CFTs could host fermionic defect operators at their endpoints and junctions. Furthermore, there is a new type of TDLs, called q-type TDLs, that have no analog in bosonic CFTs. Their distinguishing feature is an extra one-dimensional Majorana fermion living on the worldline of the TDLs. The properties of TDLs in fermionic CFTs are captured in the mathematical language of the super fusion category. We propose a classification of the rank-2 super fusion categories and explicitly construct all the nontrivial ones. We derive the corresponding spin selection rules that constrain the spectrum of the defect operators. Finally, we discuss a constraint on the renormalization group flow that preserves a q-type TDL.

It goes without saying that symmetry is a central theme in theoretical physics as it provides strong constraints on the dynamics of physical systems. A textbook example is Noether's theorem in classical physics, which states that every continuous symmetry is associated with a conservation law. At the quantum level, 't Hooft anomalies of internal or spacetime symmetries give non-trivial constraints on the infrared (IR) fixed points of renormalization group (RG) flows, especially when the IR theories are strongly-coupled.
Recently, the understanding of symmetry has significantly evolved. In the modern point of view, the presence of symmetries in a quantum field theory (QFT) is equivalent to the existence of topological defects [1]. More precisely, given a global symmetry G in a Ddimensional QFT, the action of a group element g ∈ G on a local operator O is implemented by shrinking a topological defect U g inserted on a (D − 1)-sphere with the operator O placed at a point lying inside the sphere, as shown in the figure below 1 The defect U g is called a topological defect because physical observables are invariant under continuous deformations of the manifold where U g is inserted on. The group multiplication of two elements g 1 , g 2 ∈ G is realized by fusing the corresponding topological defects U g 1 and U g 2 .
With such a conceptual breakthrough, the notion of symmetry has been extended in various directions including higher-form symmetry [1], higher-group symmetry [2][3][4][5][6], and category symmetry (non-invertible symmetry) [7,8], where the last one is the main subject of this paper. A category symmetry generalizes the group structure of an ordinary symmetry by including topological defects that do not have an inverse under the fusion. The prototype example is the symmetry generated by the topological defect lines (TDLs) in the two-dimensional Ising conformal field theory (CFT), where the TDL implementing the Kramers-Wannier duality is known to be non-invertible [8][9][10][11]. The generalization from ordinary to category symmetry is expected to provide us with new tools to understand and constrain various physical systems. For instance, the generalization of 't Hooft anomaly matching condition for category symmetry had been used to constrain the RG flows between CFTs or gapped phases [8,[12][13][14][15][16][17]. Non-invertible defects also play important roles in the study of quantum gravity [18][19][20][21][22][23]. Nunan Organisation School of Public Policy University of Birmingham, Edgbaston, Birmingham NRSP Production System Peri Urban Interface Date: December 2001 Summary This report sets out the activities and key findings of a research project that aimed to generate new knowledge to fill gaps in existing knowledge bases on natural resource management in peri-urban Kumasi, particularly relating to the livelihood strategies of the poor.The research was conducted in two Phases, reflecting the need for further analysis of existing databases and reports and the need to ensure that any further fieldwork was fully justified and useful for further phases of research under the NRSP Peri-Urban Interface Production System. Phase 1 was undertaken between September 2000 and January 2001, and fieldwork in Phase 2 from February to May 2001. During Phase 1, further analyses of data were undertaken in four main areas: agricultural systems, land transactions, GIS/remote sensing and poverty and livelihoods. Most of the new information generated in Phase 1 related to a better understanding of poverty and livelihood strategies, as the analysis in this area was able to draw on previously unanalysed data sets.The key findings include: - Much land once used for agriculture has been lost to housing in all the villages studied. The extent of loss was quantified in four villages, though the time period of the loss is not given. Have you ever wondered why some graphs "cross" the x-axis while others don't? Let's go on a math adventure and discover the secret of the x-axis crossing!

Imagine you have a funny looking cake recipe given by this formula:

f(x) = (one big slice of chocolate cake + twelve small slices of vanilla cake) / (3 big plates - a little side plate)

In math language, our crazy cake recipe looks like this:

f(x) = (x² + 14x + 24) / (3x² - 11)

Now, let's say we want to find out when our cake recipe gives us... zero cakes! Yes, it sounds silly, but it's a great way to understand graphs better. To do this, we need to find where our function equals zero:

f(x) = 0

This time, though, our recipe has fractions, so we'll make them disappear by multiplying both sides with "(3 big plates - a little side plate." Just remember, when you multiply or divide something equal to something else, the equality stays the same!

So now we have:

(x² + 14x + 24) = 0 * (3x² - 11)

Which simplifies into:

x² + 14x + 24 = 0

Now, we just need to figure out when our weird cake recipe stops giving us any cakes! We notice two numbers hiding inside our equation: -2 and -12. It turns out that these two sneaky numbers will help us find our answer. Can you guess how?

If we take our equation:

x² + 14x + 24 = 0

And break it down using our two mysterious numbers, we get this:

(x + 2) × (x + 12) = 0

Magic, isn't it? Now, remember that a product is only zero if at least one factor is zero. So, let's set each factor equal to zero:

x + 2 = 0
x + 12 = 0

Solving these equations tells us that our cake recipe gives us no cakes when:

x = -2 and x = -12

11 Hiring Mistakes To Avoid

Page 2 of 2

5- Narrow talent pool

If you want to supply the company with the best possible candidate for the job, why narrow your search to a small pool, or the wrong pool at that? I can never understand why more firms do not invest in better promotional tools to attract quality people to new job openings.

Sometimes the problem is of research. A company may assume that a large ad in the city newspaper is the answer but they fail to recognize that the demographic they seek to hire from is not targeted by the print publication. The secret is to create a profile of the ideal person for the job and then do the requisite legwork and research to target that type as hard as possible. But not many go the extra mile.

6- Compulsion to over-hire

The practice was common when the tech and Internet explosion was at hand. A ton of venture capital can lead to ridiculous results, such as a bloated promotion and sales staff. Can you say Pets.com? The size of your organization may not determine your tendency to over-hire.

Multinationals may downsize on a regular basis but even a small company must beware of an unnecessary hire. The key is to justify the need for every new candidate with as many reasons as possible. Think before you let money out the door.

7- Loyalty to an acquaintance or friend

I have never been an advocate of the practice but it is as common as the cold. People love to recommend a person they know for hire and more often than not, the candidate has a good shot at a second interview on the basis of that relationship.

Avoid that critical blunder and scrutinize a familiar face with as much care as you would a stranger. In fact, I would exercise more caution in order to avoid the perception of impropriety. That way when you do hire an acquaintance or friend, there can be no question as to their legitimacy.

8- Only one interviewer in the room

One interviewer is fine for the first session. But why not have more than one person sit in for the second interview? Instill a sense of accountability and checks and balances. In addition, having another person in the room will keep the candidate on his toes more.

I guarantee that if more companies were to put the practice into place, they would be happier with their new hires at the end of the year. The decision to fill a position is too important to have it hinge on one person's direct contact with the candidate.

9- No test case for the candidate

This may not be feasible for every company or industry but for the most part, a candidate should have the opportunity to analyze a real business scenario as part of the recruitment process. Too often with senior positions, for example, the person is deemed to be "above" such a practice. I think that is deplorable. How can you hire someone based on nothing more than theoretical observation?

The corporate world has to do a better job at providing realistic test cases to new talent to evaluate before the ultimate decision is made. The final result is the most valuable tool HR can have: better than a resume and perhaps more revealing than a reference check.

10- Improper job description

If the corporate world is guilty of one hiring mistake, it is this. Inadequate and incomplete job descriptions pervert the entire recruitment chain. First of all, the wrong type of people apply for the job opening. Subsequent to that, inappropriate candidates are interviewed.

Consequently, the final choice is ill suited to the job and will be miserable at work, fail to meet expectations and disappoint executive management. The candidate will take the blame, but you and I know that the culprit is the HR staff member who wrote the description, as well as the hiring manager who was unable to provide an accurate assessment of the job in the first place. In the end, everyone loses.

11- Dismissal of candidate based on a hole in resume

The flipside to some of the errors listed so far is the outright dismissal of a person based on a minor failure to meet some specific and primitive corporate metric for new talent. I always find it a shame when a huge corporate machine (or even a small one) chews up a worthy resume because the candidate may have taken a semester off or been fired from a previous job. Try and look at the candidate as more than a piece of paper and if there is even the slightest interest on your part, get the whole story before you send that resume to the shredder.

Now get out there and fill that job opening with the best possible candidate. With time and research invested to procure the ideal match of job and talent, your company and indeed, your new hire, will become better down the road.

**Understanding Correlation, Causation, and Spurious Patterns in Data**

### **1. Correlation vs. Causation: Definitions**
- **Correlation**: A statistical measure of how closely two variables follow a straight-line relationship. For example, if variables $ x $ and $ y $ have a strong correlation, their data points cluster tightly around a line (e.g., $ y = 2x + 1 $).
- **Causation**: A direct cause-and-effect relationship where $ x $ influences $ y $. For example, if $ y = f(x) $, $ x $ is the cause, and $ y $ is the effect. However, **correlation does not imply causation**—a high correlation might exist without a causal link.

---

### **2. Why Correlation ≠ Causation**
- **Measurement Errors**: Real-world data is often noisy. Even if $ y = mx + c $, errors in measuring $ x $ and $ y $ (e.g., $ y = mx + c + \varepsilon $) can distort the observed relationship, reducing perfect correlation.
- **Spurious Correlations**: Two variables might appear correlated purely by chance or due to a third hidden factor. For example:
  - **Example 1**: Ice cream sales and drowning incidents are correlated, but the true cause is a third variable: hot weather.
  - **Example 2**: The number of firefighters at a fire correlates with fire damage, but the fire size causes both.

---

### **3. Logical Implication vs. Everyday Implication**
- **Logical Implication ($ P \Rightarrow Q $)**: If $ P $ is true, $ Q $ must also be true. For example, "If today is Friday, then it is a weekday" is logically valid.
- **Everyday Implication**: People often assume correlation implies causation, but this is a logical fallacy. Just because $ x $ and $ y $ correlate does not mean $ x $ causes $ y $.

---

### **4. Ramsey Theory and Inevitable Patterns**
Ramsey Theory (a branch of mathematics) shows that **with enough data, patterns and correlations are inevitable**, even if they are spurious. This is critical in data science, especially with "big data."

#### **Example 1: The Pigeonhole Principle**
- **Principle**: If you have more objects than boxes, at least one box must contain multiple objects.
- **Application to Data**:
  - With 1025 people surveyed about their daily moods (on a 4-category scale for 5 days), there are $ 4^5 = 1024 $ possible "week types." By the Pigeonhole Principle, **at least two people will have identical weekly mood patterns** purely by chance.
  - Even if responses are random, this guarantees a **perfect correlation** between at least two individuals' data.

#### **Example 2: The Party Problem (Ramsey Numbers)**
- **Ramsey Number $ R(3,3) = 6 $**: In any group of 6 people, there must be either 3 mutual friends or 3 mutual strangers. This illustrates how **patterns emerge inevitably** in large datasets.
- **Implication for Data Science**: With enough data points, even random datasets will exhibit apparent patterns or clusters, which might be misinterpreted as meaningful.

---

### **5. Real-World Example: Spurious Correlation in Surveys**
- **Scenario**: 1025 people rate their daily mood (Strongly Positive, Slightly Positive, Slightly Negative, Strongly Negative) for 5 days.
- **Observation**: Two people (e.g., Mary and John) have nearly identical weekly mood patterns. Their Pearson correlation coefficient is 0.984 (very high).
- **Explanation**:
  1. There are $ 4^5 = 1024 $ possible unique combinations of 5-day mood responses.
  2. By the Pigeonhole Principle, **at least two people must share the same pattern**.
  3. This high correlation is **not due to causation** but a mathematical inevitability with large datasets.

---

### **6. Implications for Data Science**
- **Big Data Challenge**: Larger datasets increase the likelihood of spurious correlations. For example, 1,000,000 data points might produce thousands of "significant" correlations by chance alone.
- **Mitigation Strategies**:
  - **Causal Inference**: Use controlled experiments (A/B tests) or statistical methods (e.g., instrumental variables) to infer causality.
  - **Domain Knowledge**: Validate correlations with expert knowledge to distinguish meaningful from spurious patterns.
  - **Cross-Validation**: Test models on independent datasets to avoid overfitting to random noise.

---

### **Key Takeaways**
1. **Correlation ≠ Causation**: Always question the underlying cause of observed relationships.
2. **Spurious Patterns Are Inevitable**: With enough data, random datasets will produce apparent patterns.
3. **Ramsey Theory**: Mathematics explains why order and patterns emerge in large datasets, even in randomness.
4. **Data Science Best Practices**: Combine statistical rigor with domain expertise to avoid false conclusions.

# Engineering Physics Questions and Answers – Lorentz Transformation Equations

1. **A rod of length 5 m is moving at a speed of 0.6c. To an observer sitting perpendicular to the direction of motion, the length appears to be ______**  
   **Answer:** a) 5 m  
   **Explanation:** In Lorentz length contraction, dimensions perpendicular to motion remain unchanged. The contraction only occurs in the direction of motion, so the observer sees the length as 5 m.  

2. **If an object reaches the speed of light, its length changes to ______**  
   **Answer:** d) Zero  
   **Explanation:** Using the length contraction formula $ l = l_0 \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} $, when $ v \to c $, $ l \to 0 $. This is physically impossible for massive objects.  

3. **A 20-year-old person travels at high speed in a rocket for 1 Earth year. Upon returning, he would be ______**  
   **Answer:** c) A few months older  
   **Explanation:** Time dilation occurs: $ \Delta t = \frac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}} $. For the traveler, time slows, so 1 Earth year ≈ few months for them.  

4. **A rod moving at speed $ v $ appears shorter. If its direction changes by 180°, the observed length ______**  
   **Answer:** c) Remains the same  
   **Explanation:** Length contraction depends on $ v^2 $, so reversing direction (negative $ v $) does not affect the contraction.  

5. **An object of length 1 m moves at 0.5c. To an observer at rest relative to the object, the length is ______**  
   **Answer:** c) 1 m  
   **Explanation:** If the observer is at rest relative to the object, there is no relative motion, so no contraction occurs.  

6. **How fast must a rocket move for its length to contract to 95% of its original length?**  
   **Answer:** c) 0.3c  
   **Explanation:**  
   $$
   l = 0.95l_0 = l_0 \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} \implies 0.95^2 = 1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2} \implies \frac{v^2}{c^2} = 0.0975 \implies v \approx 0.3c
   $$  

7. **A cube with proper length $ l_0 $ moves at speed $ v $. The observed volume is ______**  
   **Answer:** b) $ l_0^3 \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} $  
   **Explanation:** Only one dimension contracts, so volume becomes $ l_0^2 \cdot l_0 \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}} $.  

8. **A rod of length 1 m moves at 0.5c. What is the percentage contraction in length?**  
   **Answer:** b) 14%  
   **Explanation:**  
   $$
   l = 1 \cdot \sqrt{1 - (0.5)^2} = \sqrt{0.75} \approx 0.86 \, \text{m} \implies \text{Contraction} = (1 - 0.86)/1 \times 100\% = 14\%
   $$  

9. **A particle with a proper lifetime of $ 2 \times 10^{-6} $ s moves at 0.9c. Its observed lifetime is ______**  
   **Answer:** c) $ 4.6 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{s} $  
   **Explanation:**  
   $$
   \Delta t = \frac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{\sqrt{1 - (0.9)^2}} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.436} \approx 4.6 \times 10^{-6} \, \text{s}
   $$  

10. **All particles have a proper lifetime of 1 μs. Which will survive the longest?**  
    **Answer:** d) D (fastest particle)  
    **Explanation:** Time dilation $ \Delta t = \frac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}} $ increases as $ v \to c $. The fastest particle (D) has the longest observed lifetime.

Dental disease is a HUGE deal. Periodontal (gum) disease is the number one diagnosed problem in dogs and cats. By the age of just two, 80% of dogs and 70% of cats have some form of periodontal disease. In addition, 10% of dogs have a broken tooth with pulp (nerve or root canal) exposure. This is extremely painful until the nerve dies, at which point the tooth becomes infected! Infectious oral diseases affecting the gums and root canals create systemic bacteremia (bacteria in the bloodstream, which can infect other parts of the body). Periodontal inflammation and infection have been linked to numerous problems including heart attacks, strokes, kidney disease, emphysema, liver disease, osteoporosis, pregnancy problems, and diabetes. Therefore, oral infectious diseases are known as “the silent killer.”

In addition to systemic effects, oral disease can also cause inflammation to the eye, resulting in blindness. Furthermore, jaw bone loss from chronic infection can lead to a jaw fracture known as a pathologic fracture, and these have a very hard time healing. Finally, infectious oral disease can result in osteomyelitis (an area of dead, infected bone), nasal infections and an increased risk of oral cancer.

Speaking of oral cancer, the oral cavity is the fourth most common place for cancer. Unfortunately, by the time that most are discovered, they are too advanced for therapy. Early treatment is necessary for cure. That’s why you, the pet owner, need to check your pet for oral growths on a regular basis. Anything suspicious should be shown to your veterinarian promptly.

In cats, a very common problem is feline tooth resorption lesions, which are caused by normal cells called odontoblasts eating away at the cat’s own teeth. Approximately half of the cats over 6 years of age have at least one. They are similar to cavities in that once they are advanced, they are VERY painful and can become infected. They are first seen as small red areas along the gumline.

Other oral problems include bacterial cavities, painful orthodontic problems, dead teeth (which are commonly discolored), and worn teeth. Almost every pet has some form of a painful or infectious oral disease that needs treatment. Unfortunately, there are few to no obvious clinical signs. (See below, What are the warning signs of periodontal disease?) Therefore, be proactive and ask your veterinarian for a complete oral exam, and perform regular monitoring at home.

The prime number theorem is PRA-provable

Olivier Sudac

Équipe de logique mathématique, Université Paris 7 - CNRS URA 753 and LLAIC,
Université d’Auvergne-Clermont 1, France

Abstract

We introduce several theories the language of which is rich enough to talk about usual objects of real and complex analysis, and the axioms of which allow to recover a lot of classical results (sometimes with slight modifications). We prove that these theories are conservative extensions of primitive recursive arithmetic (PRA) and develop analysis within them. Moreover, as an example of their efficiency, we shall prove that the prime number theorem is PRA-provable. © 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

Résumé

On introduit plusieurs théories dont le langage est assez riche pour parler des objets usuels de l’analyse réelle et complexe, et dont les axiomes permettent de retrouver beaucoup de résultats classiques, avec parfois quelques modifications. On montre que ces théories sont des extensions conservatrices de l’Arithmétique Primitive Récursive (PRA). Enfin, à titre d‘exemple de leur intérêt, on montre que le théorème des nombres premiers est PRA-prouvâble. © 2001 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

Keywords: Primitive recursive arithmetic; Recursive analysis; Analytical number theory

1. Introduction

Number theory has been developed since Euler making a great use of analysis, which seems to be essential. If the introduction of such transcendent methods to elucidate properties of the structure \((\mathbb{N}, +, \cdot, \leq)\) are incomparably effective, the question remains to know whether the theorems are provable in a formal theory such as Peano arithmetic (PA) or, better, in some fragments of PA, in particular within the primitive recursive arithmetic (PRA).

Mints [10] presents a system which is equivalent to PRA, and insures that the prime number theorem is provable in this system without giving details on how to deal with analysis.

Takeuti [17] gives a conservative extension of PA, called FA (finite-type arithmetic), which uses a language with higher types of variables to talk about reals, real functions, and so on, and allows to recover the elementary results of real and complex analysis, and it seems, as the author says, most of the theorems of analytical number theory. Independently, Cegielski [3, 4] had provided a complete proof in PA of the Dirichlet’s Theorem about infinity of prime numbers in an arithmetic progression, by constructing, from any model of PA, some sets of definable objects (in the language of PA), such as “real” and “complex” numbers with which he mimics real analysis. In [5], Cegielski refines this technique to write out a detailed proof of the provability within PRA of the same theorem: this is more difficult because, for example, a property as essential as the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem disappears.

Following the work of Cegielski, we introduce an increasing sequence of (conservative extensions of) first-order arithmetical theories $R\Sigma^0_\mu$, starting with $R\Sigma^0_1 = PRA$. The language of these theories allows faithful expression of the usual analytical objects. Many classical results can be reconstructed in these theories – with some slight modifications. Of course, not all of them since computable analysis (such as presented in [Abe] [11]) is a model of $R\Sigma^0_1$ and brings its share of counter-examples.

In particular, we show how we can develop “elementary” complex analysis (Cauchy’s theorem on residues...), and, on the precise example of the prime number theorem, how these tools can mimic analytical number theory, in a way sufficient to prove this theorem.

# Define the DjangoAdminLog model with appropriate field types and constraints
class DjangoAdminLog(models.Model):
    """
    Model representing the admin log entries in the Django application.
    
    Attributes:
        action_time (datetime): The timestamp when the action was performed.
        object_id (str, optional): The ID of the object affected by the action.
        object_repr (str): A string representation of the object.
        action_flag (int): The flag indicating the type of action performed.
        change_message (str): A message describing the changes made.
    """
    id: int = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    action_time: models.DateTimeField = models.DateTimeField()
    object_id: str = models.TextField(blank=True, null=True)
    object_repr: str = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    action_flag: int = models.SmallIntegerField()
    change_message: str = models.TextField()

    class Meta:
        db_table = 'django_admin_log'


# Define the Person model with appropriate field types and constraints
class Person(models.Model):
    """
    Model representing a person in the system.
    
    Attributes:
        person_id (int): The unique identifier for the person.
        first_name (str): The first name of the person.
        last_name (str): The last name of the person.
        birth_year (int): The year the person was born.
    """
    person_id: int = models.IntegerField(primary_key=True, db_column='Id')
    first_name: str = models.CharField(db_column='FirstName', max_length=50)
    last_name: str = models.CharField(db_column='LastName', max_length=50)
    birth_year: int = models.IntegerField(db_column='Year')

    class Meta:
        db_table = 'Person'


# Define the Image model with a one-to-one relationship to Person
class Image(models.Model):
    """
    Model representing an image associated with a person.
    
    Attributes:
        person (Person): The person associated with the image.
        image (File): The image file.
    """
    person: Person = models.OneToOneField(Person, on_delete=models.CASCADE, primary_key=True, db_column='id')
    image: models.ImageField = models.ImageField(upload_to='images/')

    class Meta:
        db_table = 'Image'


# Define the Position model with a foreign key relationship to Person
class Position(models.Model):
    """
    Model representing a position held by a person.
    
    Attributes:
        person (Person): The person holding the position.
        title (str, optional): The title of the position.
        age (int, optional): The age of the person at the time of the position.
        email (str, optional): The email address of the person.
        phone_number (str, optional): The phone number of the person.
    """
    person: Person = models.ForeignKey(Person, on_delete=models.CASCADE, primary_key=True, db_column='positionId')
    title: str = models.CharField(blank=True, null=True, max_length=20)
    age: int = models.IntegerField(blank=True, null=True)
    email: str = models.EmailField(blank=True, null=True, max_length=150)
    phone_number: str = models.CharField(blank=True, null=True, max_length=15)

    class Meta:
        db_table = 'position'


# Define the Worker model with a foreign key relationship to Person
class Worker(models.Model):
    """
    Model representing a worker in the system.
    
    Attributes:
        person (Person): The person who is a worker.
        department (Department): The department where the worker is employed.
        corporation (str, optional): The corporation where the worker is employed.

    person: Person = models.ForeignKey(Person, on_delete=models.CASCADE, primary_key=True, db_column='department')
